notes:
Now Ellicott.I've written notes on all 23 verses below. They draw on a smaller set of sources than you asked for, because my search and fetch tools hit their usage limit early on. I read two commentaries in full: Enduring Word (David Guzik) and Ellicott. For the rest (Wesley, Pulpit Commentary, Matthew Henry, Poole, Clarke, Newell, the Biblical Illustrator, Precept Austin, Bible Hub's combined verse pages, GotQuestions, Desiring God and The Gospel Coalition), I only had the excerpts the search tool returned.

**What's missing:**
- **No Catholic or Orthodox sources.** I couldn't reach newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **No modern scholarship.** I couldn't reach netbible.org's notes or bibleodyssey.org.
- **No Lutheran or Pentecostal sources.** Nothing from lcms.org, 1517.org, samstorms.org, pneumareview.com or ag.org.
- **No prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace material.** I found none.
- **Some quotes have no named author.** Bible Hub's combined pages (romans/14-5, 14-14 and 14-23) mix several older writers. Where the excerpt didn't name the writer, I say "a commentator on this page" rather than guess. In particular, I don't name who wrote the v. 5 Lord's Day comment.

---

## Romans 14 – Notes

**v. 1**
- In Paul's terms the "weak" believer is the stricter one. They're weak because of a legalistic outlook, not because of what they eat, and they probably thought of themselves as the strong ones. Spiritual maturity shouldn't be a condition for fellowship, and being weak is different from being rebellious. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Being "weak in the faith" means focusing on small details, each judged on its own, instead of by one central principle. "Doubtful disputations" is better rendered as criticising someone's scruples. The strong should be gentle and not draw the weak into hair-splitting debates. (Ellicott) https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: the weak person is weak "through needless scruples," and should be welcomed into fellowship with love and courtesy, not into arguments over doubtful points. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: Paul still allows no denial of basic doctrine (see Galatians 1:6–10), but he urges broad tolerance on matters that don't touch the foundation. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/14.htm
- Ray Stedman (quoted on Precept Austin) says the NIV's "whose faith is weak" is misleading. The issue is being weak in *the* faith, meaning not yet understanding the truth. Steven Cole adds that the Greek has the article, and that this person still trusts Christ and isn't confused about the gospel. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_14_word_studies
- Clarke takes the weak believer to be the converted Jew. He's welcomed into fellowship, but arguments about religion are to be avoided. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/romans/14.htm

**v. 2**
- Guzik: the abstainers may have feared meat offered to idols (compare 1 Corinthians 8), or kept Jewish food laws. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Ellicott: "believeth he may eat" is better put as "has confidence to eat." This person's faith keeps their conscience at ease. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: we can't say for certain who these people were. It reports the view of Origen, Chrysostom and others: Jewish believers still bound in conscience to the Law gave up all meat so their avoidance of pork wouldn't stand out. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/14.htm

**v. 3**
- Ellicott: each side has its typical fault. The strong look down on the weak; the weak condemn the strong. "God hath received him" refers to God taking the person into His church at baptism. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: the strong look down on the scrupulous as superstitious, and the weak judge the strong as irreverent. God has still received them "into the number of his children." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Matthew Henry: there is usually fault on both sides. Paul brings the two together through mutual forbearance, not by excommunicating either one. If God has accepted someone, we shouldn't dare reject them. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_014.cfm

**v. 4**
- Ellicott: this verse is aimed at the weak. "Stand or fall" is courtroom language for the Master's (Christ's) verdict. The better manuscripts read "the Lord," not "God," is able to make him stand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Pulpit Commentary hears indignation in "Who are you?", like Paul's tone toward the Judaisers in Galatia. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/14.htm
- Guzik: Paul isn't telling them to erase their differences, but to rise above them. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Newell: the verse defends the stronger believer against secret or open judging by those who don't share his faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/newell/romans/14.htm

**v. 5 – where traditions differ: does this include the Sabbath or Lord's Day?**
- Guzik: adding "days" shows Paul is giving principles that apply beyond food. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Wesley (Methodist): the days in view are "new moons, and other Jewish festivals." "Fully persuaded" means being sure a thing is lawful before doing it. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican): reading this with Galatians 4:10 and Colossians 2:16, keeping special days has "no absolute sanction." It's a question of religious usefulness. That is still enough reason to keep them, and he favours his own church's calendar. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: probably Jewish law days in general. To Paul, keeping them or not was unimportant in itself. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/14.htm
- A commentator on Bible Hub's combined page (not named in the excerpt) holds that Paul means Jewish days only. On this view the weak kept a day for the day's sake, as if a law still required it. The strong also kept the Lord's Day, but for the sake of worship. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/14-5.htm
- Bible Hub's Q&A takes a middle line. "Day" has no article, so the weekly Sabbath is probably included. The principle of rest from the fourth commandment remains, but which day is a matter of conscience and shouldn't be bound on anyone. https://biblehub.com/q/Romans_14_5_s_role_in_Sabbath_debate.htm
- GotQuestions: Christians are free to keep a Saturday Sabbath if they feel led to, but shouldn't judge those who don't. Each Christian decides whether to observe a Sabbath rest. https://www.gotquestions.org/Sabbath-keeping.html ; https://www.gotquestions.org/Saturday-Sunday.html
- Vincent: "every day alike" doesn't fit the Greek well; the word "alike" was added by translators. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/14-5.htm

**v. 6**
- Ellicott: the clause about the one who does *not* observe the day isn't in the best manuscripts. Saying grace makes the meal holy to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- The BSB footnote likewise says this clause appears only in the Byzantine and Textus Receptus texts. https://biblehub.com/romans/14.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: both sides are assumed to want equally to serve God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: both act "out of a principle of conscience toward God." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Steven Cole: in non-essentials, motive is what matters most. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_144-6

**vv. 7–8**
- Ellicott: an argument from the greater to the lesser. If the Christian's whole life and even death belong to Christ, so does his food. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: living "to himself" means being at one's own disposal and doing one's own will. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Matthew Henry: denying self is the "first lesson," and all true Christians share it, weak or strong. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_014.cfm
- Guzik: our lives are bound up with other lives ("No man is an island"). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/

**v. 9**
- Ellicott: the best manuscripts simply say "died and lived." The longer KJV wording is a later explanatory addition. Christ was enthroned with universal rule through the resurrection. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm

**v. 10**
- Guzik: "judge" is the strict person's sin and "show contempt" is the free person's. His source, Chuck Smith, says the judgment seat (*bema*) is about rewards, not salvation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary: the true reading is the judgment seat "of God," not "of Christ." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: up to here Paul has spoken to the weak; now he turns to the strong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Stott (quoted on Precept Austin) lists four truths behind Paul's command: God has accepted them, Christ is Lord of all, they are our brothers and sisters, and all will stand before God. https://temp.preceptaustin.org/index.php/romans_1410-12

**v. 11**
- Ellicott: Paul quotes Isaiah 45:23 from memory, putting "As I live" in place of "I have sworn by Myself." The verb can mean "confess" or "praise." Most prefer "praise," but Ellicott thinks "confess" suits v. 12 better. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: Christ is here called both Lord and God, since He is the one we live and die to. He adds a prayer for mercy on those who have differed from us. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm

**v. 12**
- Precept Austin's notes: we are judged by Christ's standards, not each other's, and each person gives account only for himself. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1410-12

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: there's a play on "judge." Use your judgment on your own conduct, not as criticism of others. "Occasion to fall" is the Greek word behind our "scandal"; it properly means a trap. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: the stumbling block is pressing someone to copy you against their conscience. The "scandal" is provoking them to hate or judge you. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Guzik: this doesn't rule out correction on clear Scripture. And you can trip up a brother either by legalism or by careless use of your freedom. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Poole: from here Paul speaks mainly to the strong. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/romans/14.htm

**v. 14**
- Ellicott: Paul sides with the less scrupulous group, and "in the Lord Jesus" is a solemn oath-like phrase. Uncleanness is in the mind of the person, not in the thing, but for that person it is real and should be treated as real. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley thinks Paul may have known this "by a particular revelation." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Matthew Henry: the persuasion rests on Christ's death, which removed the curse and ended the ban on certain foods. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_014.cfm
- Steven Cole: "nothing" is limited by the context. Scripture's clear moral commands still stand. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_1413-15

**v. 15 – where traditions differ: can a believer be destroyed?**
- Wesley (Methodist/Arminian) draws the conclusion outright: this shows that someone for whom Christ died may be destroyed. He reads "grieved" as wounded, that is, led into sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican) sees two stages: being pained, then being led to act against conscience and so "morally ruined," with Christ's work for him "cancelled." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Matthew Henry (Presbyterian) is more guarded. Drawing a soul into sin "threatens" its destruction. You destroy him "as much as in thee lies," possibly tempting him back into Judaism. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_014.cfm
- I didn't find a Reformed or Baptist writer in my sources who directly answers Wesley's conclusion.
- Guzik: if Jesus gave His life for that brother, I can give up a steak dinner. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/

**v. 16**
- Ellicott: "your good" is your Christian liberty. It shouldn't cause accusations that look bad to outsiders. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: your "good and lawful liberty." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm

**v. 17 – what kind of "righteousness"?**
- Ellicott: it isn't imputed righteousness. It's the Christian's own moral uprightness, with peace meaning harmony with others. The distinctively Christian feature is "joy in the Holy Ghost." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Poole gives both readings, imputed or inner holiness, and leans toward inner holiness. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: "the kingdom of God" means true religion, and righteousness is "the image of God stamped on the heart." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Matthew Henry: peace with others, and spiritual joy that the Spirit works in the heart. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_014.cfm
- Newell: this verse sweeps away human traditions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/newell/romans/14.htm

**v. 18**
- Ellicott: the better reading is "in this way." Such a person avoids being spoken against, as rigid legalists and anti-legalists often are. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: "men" here means wise and good men. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm

**v. 19**
- Ellicott: the best manuscripts have "so then we pursue." "Edify" means mutual building up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: practical teaching builds up; arguing over doctrine does so less directly, though sometimes it can't be avoided. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Precept Austin's notes: "pursue" pictures a runner, and the present tense makes it a lifestyle. https://www.preceptaustin.org/romans_14_notes_pt3

**v. 20**
- Ellicott and the Pulpit Commentary: "destroy" here is a different word from v. 15. It means "pull down," the opposite of "build up." "The work of God" is the Christian character grace is forming. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/romans/14.htm
- Wesley: the work God builds in the soul by faith, and in the church by harmony. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
- Clarke: don't hold back the gospel's progress, or drive a brother to abandon the faith. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/romans/14.htm

**v. 21**
- Guzik: this is about a sincere conscience stumbling, not giving in to legalists. Paul refused the circumcision demand. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Ellicott: "or is offended, or is made weak" is probably a later addition. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Poole: we should give up even things the law doesn't forbid, rather than cause offence. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/romans/14.htm
- Wesley explains the three terms as copying against conscience, losing peace, and wavering. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm

**v. 22**
- Ellicott: the better reading is "the faith which thou hast." Keep it between you and God, and don't flaunt it where it may harm others. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- Poole: this is faith about non-essential things; the basics of the faith must always be confessed openly. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/romans/14.htm
- Guzik applies the second half to things God may be asking us to give up. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Clarke: no one has peace who sins against conscience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/romans/14.htm

**v. 23 – where traditions differ: how far does "not of faith is sin" reach?**
- The narrow reading:
  - Wesley: anything done without being fully sure it's lawful is sin to that person. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/wes/romans/14.htm
  - Matthew Henry: whatever is done without clear persuasion that it's lawful; this gives conscience no power to change the act itself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Rom/Rom_014.cfm
  - Poole and Clarke say much the same. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/romans/14.htm ; https://biblehub.com/commentaries/clarke/romans/14.htm
- Ellicott (Anglican) limits the principle to cases of a doubting conscience. He says Augustine was wrong to argue from it that even good acts by unbelievers are sin. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/ellicott/romans/14.htm
- John Piper (Baptist/Reformed) reads it broadly. Sin is anything not rooted in trust in God, and for the unbeliever "everything you do is sin." This is close to the Augustinian reading Ellicott rejects. https://www.desiringgod.org/messages/whatever-is-not-from-faith-is-sin
- On Bible Hub's combined page, one commentator says "faith" here means the Christian faith itself. He calls Aquinas's rendering ("whatever is against conscience") too vague, saying it would need to be *Christian* conscience. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/romans/14-23.htm
- Guzik: if you can't do it in faith, it's sin for you. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/romans-14/
- Brian Bill sums it up as "when in doubt, throw it out." https://www.preceptaustin.org/sermons_by_brian_bill-4
